rv.q: Beetlejuice the musical is louche, macabre and pure, unadulterated fun, full of black-and-white grotesquerie, visual flair and near-the-knuckle jokes.

And in that role (Michael Keaton in the film) we have the exuberantly unhinged showmanship of David Fynn (Olivier Award-nominated for School Of Rock). Hannah Nordberg, as Lydia, is a real find. There’s instant chemistry between her and Fynn, who sports a black-and-white striped costume that makes him look like a convict zebra on the lam.
But this undead scene-stealer stops us from taking the actual narrative here seriously; we don’t have space to feel the aching poignancy just beneath its surface.
It’s just a shame that a good proportion of the lyrics were lost in the sound mix, at least where I was sitting.
The numbers are entertaining but oddly unmemorable.
But gradually the thin yet complicated plot begins to stall and sag, and the spiky script, ingenious design and sheer gutsy energy of the cast aren’t enough to compensate.
The show has a lot in its favour – not least daft entertainment value – but it lacks essential spark.
Tightly scripted, tightly choreographed, tightly delivered and for all that, with its great tunes it manages to feel fresh and crisply improvised.
In embracing its chaos while grounding its heart, Beetlejuice The Musical proves itself more than a cult import.

David Korins’ set design delivers a phantasmagoric haunted house packed with illusions, spooky projections, a gigantic puppet sandworm, oddly random explosives, and more special effects than you can shake a skeleton at. Kenneth Posner’s gorgeous purple-and-gold-led lighting design is as good as you will see anywhere in the West End.
Overall, however, it wasn’t a show that emotionally or psychologically connected with me.
An entertaining night out, but not a memorable one.
I'm left voting 'Miss' rather than 'Hit', despite the best efforts of Miss Nordberg.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this loud, brash Broadway import—some find it energetic fun with sharp performances and spectacular visuals, while others dismiss it as exhausting, heartless spectacle that prioritizes noise over substance.
